steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our measurement paper comparing commercial 5G and 4G networks in the low and mid bands. Motivate why we need to know where 5G's gains come from, state our research questions, describe the drive-test measurement campaign, and summarize our main findings as a numbered list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- 5G promise and the open question of where its gains come from
- Focus and research questions
- Measurement campaign
- Summary of findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - 5G New Radio (NR): cornerstone for AR/VR, remote driving, cloud gaming
  - our recent measurements (cite): good coverage -> avg downlink 700 Mbps (peak \sim 1 Gbps) even driving in urban areas; far beyond 4G LTE
  - possible reasons: massive MIMO (cite), beamforming (cite), higher modulation (cite), increased bandwidth
  - mid-band (1–6 GHz) crucial, balances coverage with bandwidth (cite)
  - some advanced features still in development or skipped due to cost
  - phased deployment: no earlier results on latest NR in BRS-band (2.5–2.7 GHz) and C-band (3.7–4.2 GHz)
  - need to quantify 5G spectral utilization -> should more spectrum go to mobile broadband?
- Focus / questions
  - physical layer of 4G and 5G; deployed radio channel characteristics and impact on throughput
  - low-band (< 1 GHz) and mid-band; recent NR in BRS (cite) and C-band (cite)
  - Qs: similarities/differences in channel resources and radio technologies? 5G boost mainly bandwidth or other enhancements? quantify relationship and contribution to throughput?
  - could prompt reevaluation of mobile network evolution, insights for 6G
- Measurements
  - Minneapolis and Chicago + connecting highways (Fig. 1)
  - commercial smartphones as UE; professional network analyzer logs network events and KPIs
  - > 1200 km driving; 4G + 5G of AT&T (ATT), T-Mobile (TMO), Verizon (VZW) (Table I, § III)
  - one of first comprehensive city-wide studies spanning two cities, 5G vs 4G, low/mid-bands
- Findings
  - (1) NR vs LTE throughput (§ IV-C): NR mid-band best in DL and UL; after normalization, higher bandwidth is major factor, not new 5G features; similar for uplink, not presented
  - (2) deployment density + beamforming (§ IV-B): base station (BS) density of three carriers and beamforming modes; denser + more beams in mid-band -> better signal strength -> better spectral efficiency
  - (3) signal parameters vs normalized DL throughput (§ IV-D): RSRP, MCS, CQI; NR similar to LTE; no 1024-QAM (3GPP Release 17)
  - (4) MIMO (§ IV-E): Rank Indicator (RI) -> marginal NR gain over LTE in channel rank and layers; no MU-MIMO yet in studied cities
  - (5) latency NR-SA vs NR-NSA vs LTE, T-Mobile (§ IV-C, § IV-F): only TMO has wide NR-SA; mid-band NR-SA best latency: lower signaling overhead than NR-NSA + denser mid-band deployments

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
5G New Radio (NR) networks are widely seen as the cornerstone of new next-generation mobile applications like AR/VR, remote driving, and cloud gaming. Our recent measurement studies show that when coverage is good, current commercial 5G networks can reach an average downlink throughput of 700 Mbps (with peaks of \sim 1 Gbps), even when driving in urban environments, which is far beyond what 4G Long-Term Evolution (LTE) networks do. This big improvement may come from the use of advanced wireless communication technologies, for example massive MIMO, beamforming, higher modulation, and more bandwidth. The mid-band spectrum (1–6 GHz) is thought to be especially important for the success of 5G, because it balances coverage and bandwidth. But some advanced 5G technologies may still be in product development, or they may be skipped completely because of cost. Also, because commercial 5G is deployed in phases, earlier research has no results on the latest 5G deployments in the BRS-band (2.5–2.7 GHz) and C-band (3.7–4.2 GHz). It is important to quantify the spectral utilization of 5G to decide whether more spectrum should be allocated to mobile broadband.

So in this paper we focus on the physical layer of 4G and 5G networks. We explore the characteristics of the deployed radio channels and how they affect throughput performance, with emphasis on the low-band (< 1 GHz) and mid-band channels, and especially the recent NR deployments in BRS and C-band. We want to answer these questions: What are the similarities and differences in the channel resources and radio technologies used now in 4G and 5G networks? More importantly, is the 5G performance boost mainly from more bandwidth, or do other new enhancements play big roles? And can we quantify how they relate to throughput and how much they contribute? We think answering these questions can lead to a reevaluation of how mobile networks evolve, and give useful insights for designing and deploying future 6G networks.

- Measurement campaign
  - Minneapolis and Chicago plus highways between them (Fig. 1)
  - commercial smartphones as UE, professional network analyzer logging network events and KPIs
  - over 1200 km driving; 4G and 5G of AT&T (ATT), T-Mobile (TMO), Verizon (VZW) (Table I, § III)
  - one of the first city-wide studies across two cities on 5G vs 4G in low/mid-bands
- Findings
  - (1) NR vs LTE throughput (§ IV-C): mid-band NR best; normalized -> bandwidth is the main factor, not new features; uplink similar
  - (2) density + beamforming (§ IV-B): denser BSs and more beams in mid-band -> better signal strength, spectral efficiency
  - (3) RSRP, MCS, CQI vs normalized throughput (§ IV-D): NR similar to LTE; no 1024-QAM from 3GPP Release 17
  - (4) MIMO via RI (§ IV-E): marginal NR gain; no MU-MIMO deployed
  - (5) latency for T-Mobile NR-SA / NR-NSA / LTE (§ IV-C, § IV-F): mid-band NR-SA best, less signaling overhead + denser deployment

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
5G New Radio (NR) networks are widely seen as the cornerstone of new next-generation mobile applications like AR/VR, remote driving, and cloud gaming. Our recent measurement studies show that when coverage is good, current commercial 5G networks can reach an average downlink throughput of 700 Mbps (with peaks of \sim 1 Gbps), even when driving in urban environments, which is far beyond what 4G Long-Term Evolution (LTE) networks do. This big improvement may come from the use of advanced wireless communication technologies, for example massive MIMO, beamforming, higher modulation, and more bandwidth. The mid-band spectrum (1–6 GHz) is thought to be especially important for the success of 5G, because it balances coverage and bandwidth. But some advanced 5G technologies may still be in product development, or they may be skipped completely because of cost. Also, because commercial 5G is deployed in phases, earlier research has no results on the latest 5G deployments in the BRS-band (2.5–2.7 GHz) and C-band (3.7–4.2 GHz). It is important to quantify the spectral utilization of 5G to decide whether more spectrum should be allocated to mobile broadband.

So in this paper we focus on the physical layer of 4G and 5G networks. We explore the characteristics of the deployed radio channels and how they affect throughput performance, with emphasis on the low-band (< 1 GHz) and mid-band channels, and especially the recent NR deployments in BRS and C-band. We want to answer these questions: What are the similarities and differences in the channel resources and radio technologies used now in 4G and 5G networks? More importantly, is the 5G performance boost mainly from more bandwidth, or do other new enhancements play big roles? And can we quantify how they relate to throughput and how much they contribute? We think answering these questions can lead to a reevaluation of how mobile networks evolve, and give useful insights for designing and deploying future 6G networks.

For this we did extensive in-field measurements in two major metropolitan areas in the US, Minneapolis and Chicago, and on the highways between them, as shown in Fig. 1. We use commercial smartphones as user equipment (UE) and a professional network analyzer tool to log all network events and key performance indicators (KPIs). Our data covers a driving distance of more than 1200 km and includes both 4G and 5G networks of three major US operators, AT&T (ATT), T-Mobile (TMO), and Verizon (VZW), as shown in Table I (see § III for details). As far as we know, our work is one of the first comprehensive city-wide studies across two cities that looks at the improvements of 5G over 4G, focusing on the low- and mid-bands.

We analyzed these datasets in depth, and our conclusions are:

(1) Throughput performance of NR vs. LTE (§ IV-C): We compare throughput over representative low- and mid-band channels in NR and LTE. As expected, the NR mid-band channels do very well in downlink and uplink compared to the other NR and LTE channels. But when we normalize the throughput, we show that the higher channel bandwidth of mid-band 5G is a major reason for the higher throughput, and not the new 5G features. The uplink throughput results are similar, so we don't present them separately.

(2) Impact of deployment density and beamforming on downlink throughput (§ IV-B): We compare the density of base stations (BSs) deployed by the three carriers and the beamforming modes they use. Denser deployments and more beams in the mid-band give better overall signal strength and so better spectral efficiency.

(3) Contribution of different 4G and 5G signal parameters to normalized downlink throughput (§ IV-D): We also analyze how signal parameters like Reference Signal Received Power (RSRP), Modulation Coding Scheme (MCS), and Channel Quality Indicator (CQI) contribute to the normalized throughput. These parameters in NR behave similarly to the ones in LTE. We also see that 1024-QAM modulation, which was introduced in the latest 3GPP Release 17, is not there.

(4) MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output) performance in NR vs. LTE (§ IV-E): Comparing the Rank Indicator (RI) value shows only a marginal increase in NR MIMO performance over LTE, in terms of the actual channel rank and the number of layers the physical channel can support. Multi-User MIMO (MU-MIMO) is also not deployed yet in the cities we studied.

(5) Latency of NR-SA (Standalone), NR-NSA (Non-Standalone), and LTE networks in low- and mid-bands for T-Mobile (§ IV-C, § IV-F): T-Mobile is the only operator that has widely deployed NR-SA, so we compared latency for NR-SA, NR-NSA, and LTE. Mid-band NR-SA has the best latency, because it has lower signaling overhead (compared to NR-NSA) and the mid-band deployments are denser.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
5G New Radio (NR) networks are widely recognized as the cornerstone for emerging next-generation mobile applications such as AR/VR, remote driving, and cloud gaming. Our recent measurement studies [1] reveal that with good coverage, current commercial 5G networks can achieve an average downlink throughput of 700 Mbps (with peak rates reaching \sim 1 Gbps) even while driving in urban environments, far surpassing 4G Long-Term Evolution (LTE) networks. This substantial improvement may be attributed to advanced wireless communication technologies, including massive MIMO [2], beamforming [3], higher modulation [4], and increased bandwidth. The mid-band spectrum (1–6 GHz) in particular is considered crucial for the success of 5G, as it balances coverage with bandwidth [5]. However, some advanced 5G technologies may still be in product development or skipped altogether due to cost considerations. Additionally, due to the phased deployment of commercial 5G, earlier research has no results on the latest 5G deployments in the BRS-band (2.5–2.7 GHz) and C-band (3.7–4.2 GHz). It is essential to quantify the spectral utilization of 5G to determine whether additional spectrum should be allocated to mobile broadband.

Hence, in this paper we focus on the physical layer of 4G and 5G networks, exploring the characteristics of deployed radio channels and their impact on throughput performance, with emphasis on the low-band (< 1 GHz) and mid-band channels, particularly the recent NR deployments in BRS [6] and C-band [7,8]. Specifically, we address the following questions: What are the similarities and differences in the channel resources and radio technologies currently used in 4G and 5G networks? More importantly, is the observed 5G performance boost primarily a result of increased bandwidth, or do other novel enhancements play significant roles? And can we quantify their relationship and contribution to throughput? We believe that answering these questions can prompt a reevaluation of mobile network evolution and offer valuable insights for the design and deployment of future 6G networks.

To this end, we carried out extensive in-field measurements in two major US metropolitan areas, Minneapolis and Chicago, along with the highways connecting them, as shown in Fig. 1. We use commercial smartphones as user equipment (UE) and a professional network analyzer tool to log all network events and key performance indicators (KPIs). Our data spans a driving distance of over 1200 km and covers the 4G and 5G networks of three major US operators—AT&T (ATT), T-Mobile (TMO), and Verizon (VZW)—as shown in Table I (see § III for details). To the best of our knowledge, our work is one of the first comprehensive city-wide studies spanning two cities to assess the enhancements of 5G over 4G, with a particular focus on the low- and mid-bands.

With these datasets, we conduct an in-depth analysis and summarize our conclusions as follows:

(1) Comparison of throughput performance between NR and LTE (§ IV-C): We compare throughput over representative low- and mid-band channels in NR and LTE. As expected, NR mid-band channels perform exceedingly well in downlink and uplink compared to other NR and LTE channels. However, after normalizing the throughput, we show that the higher channel bandwidth of mid-band 5G, rather than new 5G features, is a major factor in the increased throughput. Uplink throughput shows similar results, which we therefore do not present separately.

(2) Impact of deployment density and beamforming on downlink throughput (§ IV-B): We compare the density of base stations (BSs) deployed by the three carriers and the beamforming modes used, and find that denser deployments together with more beams in the mid-band lead to better overall signal strength and hence better spectral efficiency.

(3) Analysis of the contribution of various 4G and 5G signal parameters to normalized downlink throughput (§ IV-D): We further analyze the contribution of signal parameters such as Reference Signal Received Power (RSRP), Modulation Coding Scheme (MCS), and Channel Quality Indicator (CQI) to normalized throughput, and show that these parameters in NR perform similarly to their LTE counterparts. We also note the absence of 1024-QAM modulation, introduced in the latest 3GPP Release 17.

(4) Comparison of Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) performance in NR and LTE (§ IV-E): Comparing the Rank Indicator (RI) value shows a marginal increase in NR MIMO performance over LTE in terms of actual channel rank and the number of layers the physical channel can support. We also note that Multi-User MIMO (MU-MIMO) has not yet been deployed in the cities we studied.

(5) Comparison of latency performance between NR-SA (Standalone), NR-NSA (Non-Standalone), and LTE networks in low- and mid-bands for T-Mobile (§ IV-C, § IV-F): Since T-Mobile is the only operator with widely deployed NR-SA, we compare the latency of NR-SA, NR-NSA, and LTE. Mid-band NR-SA shows the best latency owing to its lower signaling overhead (compared to NR-NSA) and denser mid-band deployments.

References:
[1] J. Carpenter, W. Ye, F. Qian, and Z.-L. Zhang, “Multi-modal vehicle data delivery via commercial 5G mobile networks: An initial study,” in 2023 IEEE 43rd International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems Workshops (ICDCSW) . IEEE, 2023, pp. 157–162.
[2] T. E. Bogale and L. B. Le, “Massive MIMO and mmWave for 5G wireless HetNet: Potential benefits and challenges,” IEEE Vehicular Technology Magazine , vol. 11, no. 1, pp. 64–75, 2016.
[3] A. N. Uwaechia and N. M. Mahyuddin, “A comprehensive survey on millimeter wave communications for Fifth-Generation Wireless Networks: Feasibility and challenges,” IEEE Access , vol. 8, pp. 62 367–62 414, 2020.
[4] 3rd Generation Partnership Project, “TS 38.214 5G; NR; Physical layer procedures for data version 17.1.0 Release 17,” 2022.
[5] Nokia, “5G spectrum bands explained,” https://www.nokia.com/thought-leadership/articles/spectrum-bands-5g-world/ , accessed: 2023-11-26.
[6] M. Dano, “The quiet brilliance of T-Mobile’s 5G spectrum strategy,” 2022, accessed: 2023-11-26. [Online]. Available: https://www.lightreading.com/5g/the-quiet-brilliance-of-t-mobile-s-5g-spectrum-strategy
[7] M. Alleven, “AT&T takes advantage of early C-band clearing,” 2023, accessed: 2023-11-26. [Online]. Available: https://www.fiercewireless.com/5g/att-takes-advantage-early-c-band-clearing
[8] K. Schulz, “Verizon turbo charges its 5G network with the addition of more spectrum,” 2023, accessed: 2023-11-26. [Online]. Available: https://www.verizon.com/about/news/verizon-5g-network-addition-more-spectrum
